newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British Business press - Nov 10.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British Business press - Nov 10.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
SUNDAY TELEGRAPH
-- GRANADA TO BREAK UP HOTELS CHAIN

Granada are set to sell off the chain of Exclusive hotels individually after receiving final bids for the 17-strong group of hotels. The news comes as Granada's advisor Lazard Brothers is struggling to find good quality buyers for all the hotels. By selling the good hotels at trophy prices Granada will be able to sell the less attractive assets cheaply and still achieve a better return overall.
-- SCOTTISH LIFE PLANS 100 MILLION STG MARKET DEBUT

One of Scotland's leading life assurers, Scottish Life, is poised to come to the stockmarket for the first time in its history by raising 100 million stg through a bond issue to bolster its free asset ration and shore up defences against bidders. The firm will start sounding out potential investors this week.
-- CABLE AND WIRELESS SET FOR ONE BILLION STG HONGKONG SALE

New chief executive of Cable and Wireless, Dick Brown, is believed to be preparing to sell down the telecommunications company's stake in its subsidiary Hongkong Telecom to below 50 per cent in return for better access to the vast Chinese telecoms market. The group said it had reached preliminary agreement with Chinese authorities on future co-operation.
-- NORTHERN MAY SELL SUPPLY ARM

As part of a defensive move against the 766 million stg bid from CalEnergy, Northern Electric is considering selling off its electricity and gas supply business for 200 million stg. The group is thought to have been approached by several other electricity companies.
-- INFLATION ADDS TO RATES FEARS

Figures to be released on Thursday are set to show that the core rate of inflation is rising to the highest level for more than two years, from 2.9 per cent to over three per cent, intensifying pressure for a further rise in interest rates. The figures will add strength to the Bank of England's inflation assessment published last week.
SUNDAY TIMES
-- SMITHKLINE BOSS TOPS 'OVERPAID' LIST

A survey of FT-SE 100 index leaders' business pay reveals that the chief executive of SmithKline Beecham, Jan Leschly, collected 13.1 million stg last year, mostly earned through gains on the stock options awarded by the drugs company.
-- BUSINESS SPLIT EVENLY OVER SINGLE CURRENCY

According to a poll, carried out by Market and Opinion Research International for the Confederation of British Industry and the British Chambers of Commerce, business is "split down the middle" over a European single currency. It suggests it will be hard to come up with a consensus view from business.
-- KOHL PRESSED ON EUROFIGHTER

Prime minister John Major, Chancellor Kenneth Clarke and defence secretary Michael Portillo have launched a diplomatic offensive to prevent Germany ending plans to start production of the Eurofighter. They are lobbying their German counter-parts before a key vote in the German parliament on Thursday. This could kill British hopes of launching the production phase of the 40 billion stg four-nation project.
-- ALLIED TO DROP DEMERGER PLAN

Allied Domecq is expected to decide against demerging its spirits and retailing businesses into two separate companies. Allied's chairman, Sir Christopher Hogg, is understood to have decided that the costs of demerger are prohibitive. His decision could result in the group's shares suffering short-term weakness.
-- HANSON TAKES 50 PER CENT PAY CUT

Lord Hanson is to announce that he is halving his salary from 1.32 million to 660,000 stg, an unprecedented amount for an executive director of a big British company. The move is in response to a four-way split at the industrial combine. Hanson was one of the first British industrialists to earn more than one million stg.
THE OBSERVER
-- BUILDING SOCIETIES FIGHT BID CURB LAW

Larger building societies gearing up to join the stock market are threatening the proposed legislation to protect small societies from takeover. The Halifax, Alliance and Leicester, Woolwich and Northern Rock, are all planning stock market flotations next year and are objecting to draft legislation outlined by the Treasury Minister Angela Knight.
-- BRITISH TELECOM 'DIAL-A-PORN' DEAL COULD RAISE US REGULATOR'S HACKLES

British Telecom could face problems from the US regulator over its involvement with a phone sex deal before its proposed merger with MCI can go ahead. BT use a system of 'short-stopping' which means numbers are diverted abroad and could lead to overcharging. The Federal Communications Commission expressed the view that this was improper.
-- LARGE COMPANIES MAY LOSE TAX BREAKS ON PRP

Chancellor Kenneth Clarke is under pressure to clamp down on the PRP tax break, which means large companies could be singled out in the Budget for tough treatment over tax relief on profit- related pay. The Treasury is looking at a plan which would separate large companies from small and medium-sized firms.
-- MYSTERIOUS MAGNATE BIDS FOR NOTTINGHAM FOREST

John Bredenkamp, former rugby player who made his fortune through his trading company Casalee, which trades tobacco, has made a bid for Premier League football club Nottingham Forest. Other bidders include a consortium led by former Tottenham Hotspur chairman Irvine Scholar, a consortium of local businessmen and a Norwegian group. Forest's board will decide which bid to recommend on Thursday.
-- HARD TIMES IN SMITH SQUARE AS COMPANIES SNUB TORIES

According to survey from Pensions and Investment Research Consultants of 289 FTSE-350 companies, the number of companies contributing to the Conservative Party has fallen. Some are due to shareholder unease, while some are due to specific events. The Conservatives still have some loyal contributors, such as P&O and Hanson.
INDEPENDENT ON SUNDAY
-- BLAIR'S NEW SALES TAX UNDER FIRE

Accountants and commerce have branded Labour Party proposals to tax small businesses on turnover rather than profits unfair and unworkable. There is concern that Tony Blair will choose to single out a turnover tax as the only specific fiscal measure to encourage small businessmen.
-- COMMISSION PROBES LONRHO'S ANGLO LINK

Lonrho's link-up with Anglo-American is being vetted by the European Commission in an enquiry which may lead to the South African mining giant being forced to sell its 26 per cent stake. The Commission's concerns are over reduced competition in the supply of platinum, if Anglo is deemed to have a significant influence on Lonrho's mining operations.
-- DOMINION PLANS 650 PENCE STG POWER BID

The US electricity and gas company, Dominion Resources, is to decide how to proceed with a 650 pence stg share bid for East Midlands Electricity. The offer values the company at 1.3 billion stg. Options include a dawn raid to grab between 10 and 20 per cent of East Midlands or a delay to see what action UK regulators take over CalEnergy's bid for Northern Electric.
-- MURDOCH TO TESTIFY AT FRAUD TRIAL

Rupert Murdoch is among current and former News International staff to be put on the stand in a fraud trial in the High Court. The inquiry is inspired by Michael Clinger, former executive, in a dispute over the alleged skimming of 20 million stg of profits from the supply of Sky TV smartcards.
-- AT&T DEMANDS MORE UK ACCESS

The US telecoms giant AT&T is pressing US regulators to demand major concessions over access to Britain's telecommunications market as a price for allowing the 35 billion stg merger between British Telecom and MCI to go ahead. AT&T's lawyers are expected to lobby for more access to the UK market during the public consultation process that follows such an application.
MAIL ON SUNDAY
-- MILK GIANT READY FOR 350 MILLION STG SALE

Northern Foods, Britain's biggest milk business, is up for sale, either by a public flotation or a trade sale, for about 350 million stg. The company controls nearly a quarter of the supply of milk in England and Wales. The move comes after the collapse of merger discussions with rival dairy and transport group Unigate.
-- 'FLAWED' CREST SYSTEM FACES DELAYS

The London Stock Exchange's new electronic share settlement system, Crest, is set to stop all transfers of stocks on to its database due to software problems and a backlog of queries. This could cost companies millions of pounds stg and several top brokers are asking for a shutdown of the system.
-- SHADOW ON HOUSE PRICES

A report by Mintel contradicts optimistic house price date issued last week by leading mortgage lenders. The survey predicts low-key prospects for property and that the value of the average home has risen by just four to five per cent in the past year and prices will continue rising at that modest rate for the next decade.
-- WALKER LOSES FOUR MILLION STG ROUND

Leisure group Brent Walker has stopped founder George Walker pushing it into collapse by blocking his plans to sue it for four million stg over his boardroom sacking in 1991. The company paid 411,000 stg to buy the right to sue for unfair dismissal from Walker's trustees in bankruptcy.
-- SAINSBURY TO OFFER INSURANCE

Sainsbury, the supermarket giant, is poised to offer general insurance direct. The retailer will offer household cover through its Homebase chain and the service may extend to supermarket outlets. The group has teamed up with UK broker Willis Corroon to provide insurance branded with the Sainsbury name. BMC +44-171-377-1742
